Growing-season bounds for each administrative division

Source: R/read_season_by_poly.R
read_season_by_poly.Rd

Summarises a published crop calendar over the cells of each division, so a division-level analysis can use a growing season as its window. The points equivalent is read_season().

Usage

read_season_by_poly(
  boundaries,
  source = "asis",
  season = 1,
  land_cover = c("cropland", "pasture"),
  stat = c("mode", "mean"),
  min_share = 0.1,
  id = NULL,
  path = NULL
)

Arguments

boundaries

A SpatVector of divisions, from read_boundaries().

source

Only "asis". GAEZ publishes no land-cover mask and no second season, so it has nothing to summarise per division that read_season() does not already give per point.

season

1 or 2.

land_cover

"cropland", "pasture", or both for cropland with pasture where cropland is absent.

stat

"mode", "mean" or both.

min_share

The share of a division's cells that must carry a season before that season describes the division. It gates whichever land cover supplies the bounds, not only the first: a division where cropland falls short falls back to pasture, and if pasture falls short too the division gets no season rather than one resting on a handful of cells.

id

Name of the division column in boundaries; ID_adm_div by default.

path

The dataset folder, if it is not in the spatial repository found by find_nested_folder().

Value

A tibble with one row per division: the division id, the requested bounds, season_share (the share of the division's cells carrying the season it was given), cropland_share, pasture_share and season_source. The unit is in the "season_unit" attribute.

Details

Two choices arise that never arise for a point, and both are recorded in the result rather than hidden:

Which statistic. A division spans many cells and rarely one calendar. stat takes "mode", "mean" or both, giving sos_mode, sos_mean and so on. The mode is the usual choice: it answers "when does this division mostly sow", and a handful of cells on another system does not move it. The mean is reported alongside because a wide gap between the two is itself the finding that a division has no single season.

Which land cover. ASIS masks its phenology to cropland ("cropland") or pasture ("pasture"). Give both, the default, and cropland governs wherever it covers at least min_share of a division's cells, with pasture taking over where it does not. That matters in pastoral areas, where the cropland mask is empty over much of the territory: without the fallback those divisions get no window and drop out of the analysis, which is selection on exactly the thing being studied. season_source records which cover each division ended up on, and cropland_share and pasture_share are both reported, so the choice can be audited or overridden.

min_share gates the cover that is actually used, which matters more than it sounds. A modal dekad over whatever cells survive the flag mask will describe a division from a single cell if that is all there is, and the value will look perfectly ordinary — a confident wrong season is harder to notice than a missing one. ASIS's second season is rare outside bimodal regimes (0.2% of Niger's cells carry one, against 29% for the first), so without the gate season = 2 returns a plausible-looking window for nearly every division in a unimodal country.

ASIS defines the end of season with a different NDVI threshold on cropland than elsewhere, so eos from the two covers is not strictly the same quantity; sos is less affected. Read season_source before comparing season lengths across divisions.

Bounds are dekads, signed and linear from 1 January: a second season reaching into the next year is 40, not 4, and one starting in the previous year is negative. Pass unit = "dekad" to window_calendar().

See also

read_season(), window_calendar()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
divisions <- read_boundaries(path, iso = "NER", level = 2)
seasons <- read_season_by_poly(divisions, season = 1)
table(seasons$season_source)
} # }
